title: The delivery payout that quietly shrinks to zero
problem: Delivery aggregators keep running ad campaigns a restaurant refused, and one stretched a 2-hour discount on 3 dishes into an all-day, full-menu offer the restaurant paid for. Payout statements stack commissions, fees and GST so densely that owners cannot tell what an order earned. A 6-outlet chain lost ₹16 lakh in small, unnotified deductions before hiring a recovery service to claw most of it back.
challenge: Catch every wrong deduction on a restaurant's delivery payout the week it lands, with the proof to claim it back.

title: Machine down and the only expert is days away
problem: Small factories halt production for days after a breakdown because nothing connects them quickly with qualified repair technicians. Skilled trades take years to learn, technicians on the floor get little real-time guidance, and many cannot even complete a work order from a phone.
challenge: Get a stalled machine diagnosed within the hour by the people already on the floor.

title: Every 5th appointment is an empty chair
problem: An audit of 47 Indian specialist practices found about 1 in 5 booked appointments end as no-shows, and few clinics even track it. A patient who wants to reschedule can only call during working hours or reply to an SMS nobody reads, so a cancellation quietly turns into an empty slot that no other patient can use.
challenge: Cut a clinic's no-shows in half without adding a single call to the front desk.

title: Cab drivers accept trips blind and earn below cost
problem: Drivers cannot see whether a trip is long or short before accepting, fares no longer cover running costs on hot days, and fees and penalties take close to 40 percent. Broken buttons and penalties for cancellations they did not cause cut earnings further.
challenge: Show a driver, before accepting, whether a trip will make or lose money after fuel and fees.

title: Hindi Shorts that stall, and nobody explains why
problem: Hindi-speaking creators see far more watch hours in their analytics than YouTube counts towards monetisation, and nothing explains the gap. Shorts reach stalls and subscriber growth stops with no word on what to change, while makers posting daily get buried under machine-made noise. Both questions were asked on YouTube's own help forum on 6 Oct.
challenge: Give a Hindi-speaking creator a weekly note, in Hindi, on what to change next and why.

title: The gateway discount that was promised and never applied
problem: Merchants on Razorpay and Cashfree report fees deducted above the rate they signed for, and one found a promised discount had never been applied, costing lakhs. Complaints go nowhere: one merchant raised a dozen tickets over 4 months and had the account deactivated before anything was fixed. Often there is no way even to see where a ticket stands.
challenge: Check every fee a merchant's gateway charged last month against the agreed rate, and recover the overcharge.

title: Interiors promised in 45 days, finished 4 months late
problem: Homeowners pay a large advance, or the whole amount upfront, then wait while interiors work starts late or never starts. Reviews of Livspace and HomeLane describe projects running months over, staff changing without handover and defects left open, and a NoBroker interiors customer was refused a refund after no work began. Once the money has moved, the family has nothing left to push with.
challenge: Keep every rupee of an interiors payment back until that stage is finished and photographed.

title: The take-home test AI can now sit for you
problem: Since 2025, take-home coding work has been easy to hand to AI, so one programming instructor moved most of the grade into in-class exams. Another educator found even recorded take-home oral exams could be gamed, leaving live, in-person checks as the only honest test. Those checks do not stretch beyond a small class, and teaching methods have barely changed in decades.
challenge: Let a teacher check, in 5 minutes per student, that whoever submitted the work actually understands it.

title: Tax notices built on UPI receipts
problem: Small traders received thousands of tax notices based purely on their UPI receipts, then were asked for years of purchase bills and statements they never kept, and some pulled their QR codes to go cash-only. Their billing software does not help, because records vanish at year-end, calculations go wrong and they still pay an accountant to redo it.
challenge: Turn a small shop's payment history into books that can answer a tax notice in a day.

title: The job post that drowns in generated applications
problem: An open job post can pull in hundreds of irrelevant, machine-generated applications within hours, so one hiring manager gave up and went back to referrals. Remote screening is no safer, with candidates quietly feeding questions to AI, and a small business running a design contest on Freelancer got over 1,000 AI-generated logos and could not get its prize money back. Referrals shut out good people with no network.
challenge: Let a small employer open a role to anyone and still find the genuine applicants by the end of the first day.

title: Size 32 at one label, 34 at the next
problem: Indian clothing brands borrowed US and UK size charts, so a 32 at one label is a 34 at another and most shoppers guess. Fashion e-commerce returns run at 25–40%, mostly for fit, and festive cash-on-delivery orders bounced 58% of the time against under 15% for prepaid. New EU rules now make retailers inspect and handle returns rather than destroy them, so every return costs more.
challenge: Cut a fashion brand's size returns by a third within one season.

title: Fake seed in a real-looking bag
problem: Counterfeit weedicide and faulty seed reach small farmers through local dealers, and the loss shows only weeks later as a dead crop. Genuine bags look overpriced next to fakes because farmers cannot check what a real product should cost, and the only route to compensation is a court case few can afford.
challenge: Let a farmer check, at the dealer's counter, that a bag of seed or spray is genuine and fairly priced.

title: Weeks of chasing a chatbot for your own money
problem: Refunds for cancelled or undelivered food orders take weeks, and chatbots block every route to a human, so customers chase support and threaten public escalation to get their money back. Those who cannot argue in English are denied outright, and restaurants owed money by the same services wait weeks through repeated escalations too.
challenge: Get people their refund from a delivery service without them writing a single complaint themselves.

title: Owed lakhs, afraid to ask the buyer for it
problem: About ₹8.1 lakh crore owed to small suppliers sits in overdue buyer payments, yet most avoid complaints for fear of losing the customer. Filing through the online dispute route means assembling invoices and evidence nobody has time for, resolution is not time-bound, and polite reminders get ignored.
challenge: Turn a supplier's overdue invoices into a ready-to-file claim in one evening, without burning the relationship.

title: Every new doctor starts from a folder of X-rays
problem: Hospitals rarely hand over digital copies, so patients carry folders of paper reports and X-rays from one doctor to the next. Complaints from January 2026 describe doctors at a new hospital unable to see past prescriptions or allergies, and an online doctor on PharmEasy advised without opening the reports the patient had uploaded. Families of a sick child bounce between hospitals with nobody pulling the records into one diagnosis.
challenge: Turn a folder of paper reports into a one-page history any new doctor can read in a minute.

title: The late ride home that starts with fear
problem: Women heading home late avoid autos and cabs, solo travellers fear being stranded in an unfamiliar city, and families avoid parks nobody can vouch for. When a ride does go wrong there is little recourse: in May 2025 a Rapido driver headed away from the railway station, and another drove abusively. Even the bike-taxi ride PIN meant to confirm the right driver never changes between trips.
challenge: Let a woman travelling late know the moment her ride goes off route, and bring help within seconds.

title: The small community losing its feed to bots
problem: Cheap AI-generated posts flooded small online communities in 2025, and they cannot filter the bots without demanding everyone's real identity. Checking uploads still needs trusted human moderators that small hosts cannot afford, so one hosting startup had to build its own checks. Meanwhile readers drown in newsletters they never signed up for, and Substack makes them open an account just to report it.
challenge: Keep a small community free of bots, spam and unsafe uploads for less than the cost of one moderator.

title: The digital arrest that ends in a UPI transfer
problem: Callers posing as officials tell people they are under digital arrest and pressure them into moving their savings over UPI before they realise it is a scam. Voice clones and deepfake video calls became cheap in 2025, so the official on the screen can look and sound real. Meanwhile elderly parents already struggle with the endless security checks meant to protect them.
challenge: Stop a digital arrest scam before the money moves, without locking the target out of their own account.

title: One flat listed, 15 calls a day, years later
problem: Free listings on 99acres and MagicBricks are throttled to near-zero views while sales teams ring owners again and again to push paid upgrades. One portal shared an owner's number with developers without consent, and a former customer still gets over 15 sales calls a day years after closing the account. Listing a home once can cost an owner their phone number for good.
challenge: Let an owner list a property without their real phone number ever reaching a sales team.

title: The sales call promised it, the course denied it
problem: Edtech sales staff promise deferrals, content and mentoring on calls, then the company denies it after payment and refuses to check the recording. Parents and students are pressured into upgrades, told their existing course is worthless, and spammed from many numbers after signing up. Complaints about coaching to the consumer helpline tripled in a year.
challenge: Make every promise on an edtech sales call show up in writing before the buyer pays.

title: Sold on paper, still waiting for the cash
problem: Small online sellers in India see about a quarter of cash-on-delivery orders come back, then wait 3–7 days for couriers to hand over the cash from the rest, which stalls restocking. Shops selling on ONDC lose 25–35% of earnings to delivery, packaging and fees, and wait 7–15 days for payouts. A month that looks profitable in the books can still run out of cash before the next stock order.
challenge: Show a small online seller which orders will turn into cash, and when, before they spend on stock or ads.

title: Nobody remembers why it was built this way
problem: Teams lose the reasoning behind past decisions, so new hires spend weeks digging through old tickets and commit history to learn why things are the way they are. Work inherited from departed colleagues arrives with no context or owner, and the meetings and customer conversations that held the answer were never captured.
challenge: Let anyone ask why a past decision was made and get the reason, the people and the date in seconds.

title: The fake moisturiser you only spot after using it
problem: Counterfeit cosmetics reach buyers through big marketplaces, and buyers often suspect a fake only after using it. In June 2026 a Nykaa buyer worked it out after the return window had closed and was refused a refund. The one reliable check is comparing the packaging with a store-bought original, and when one shopper did that, neither the brand nor the marketplace replied.
challenge: Let a buyer tell whether a beauty product is genuine within a minute of unboxing it.

title: Farmer collectives that can grow but cannot sell
problem: Farmer producer organisations default on dues and fail at marketing, with no budget for branding, weak buyer trust and part-time boards who cannot price, contract or manage cold chain. Those that list online stall on cataloguing, labelling, food-safety rules, costly rural shipping and payments that take weeks.
challenge: Let a farmer collective run its selling side without hiring a full-time trading team.

title: One inspection, no hygiene records, licence gone
problem: Small food units and farms keep hygiene, pest-control and field records on paper or in clunky software, and a single inspection is enough to expose the gaps. In September 2026 a food manufacturer lost its licence after inspectors found pests and no food-safety records. Inspection drives in Indian cities stepped up through 2025 and 2026, so the record a unit skips is the one it gets asked for.
challenge: Make a small food unit inspection-ready every day with 5 minutes of record keeping.

title: The 9 kg parcel billed as 13 kg
problem: Couriers re-weigh parcels after pickup and bill small online sellers for weight that was never there, sometimes 2–3 weeks after booking and with no photo proof. One seller's 9 kg parcel was charged as 13 kg, and Shiprocket ignored the dispute, leaving the extra charge in place. As these charges pile up, the aggregator's rates end up higher than going straight to the courier.
challenge: Give a small seller proof of weight and size that settles the dispute before it starts.

title: A parent's care, arranged from another city
problem: Sole earners living in another city find arranging care for an ageing parent fragmented and stressful. Paying someone to coordinate it is out of reach for most, and one family was quoted about $20,000 a year for concierge care coordination. One caregiver of a parent with dementia says the time and money it takes has stalled their career completely.
challenge: Let a working child keep a parent's doctors, medicines and helpers on track in 10 minutes a day.

title: Car hosts lose their income to unsettled claims
problem: People who rent out their car through sharing marketplaces wait months or a year for damage, seizure or total-loss payouts while the car sits idle. New drivers wait days for activation with no way to fix a rejected document.
challenge: Help a car host or driver build a claim the marketplace cannot ignore, and track it to payment.

title: A famous face, a fake investment link, real losses
problem: Deepfake videos of well-known public figures push fake investment links, and scams like these surged across India in 2025. Finance influencers hide conflicts or misrepresent their results, and young followers lose money acting on advice they have no easy way to check. Even an honest search for real information keeps landing on machine-made filler.
challenge: Help a young investor check a finance video's claims, and who is making them, before they act on it.

title: One gateway freeze can stop a business overnight
problem: Online merchants have accounts blocked, settlements held or collections closed by their payment provider without explanation, sometimes for months. Money already earned stays frozen, working capital vanishes, and a business relying on a single provider has nobody to call.
challenge: Keep a small online business taking payments the day its gateway freezes it.

title: The deposit you lose even with photos
problem: Renters learn about mould, pests and other hazards only after signing the lease, and new owners find seepage, cracks or termites within weeks because proper pre-purchase inspections are rare. At move-out, tenants still face heavy deductions from their deposit, photos or not. With no record of condition that both sides agreed at handover, every later argument is one word against another.
challenge: Make a dated record of a home's condition in 15 minutes that landlord and tenant both sign.

title: Half of job seekers cannot spot a fake recruiter
problem: Most Indian job seekers have met fraudulent job offers, and half cannot tell a genuine recruiter from a scammer, with the youngest hit hardest. Fake postings sit on major internship boards with no visible employer check, and fear of scams now makes young candidates ignore real opportunities. People lose registration fees and months of search time.
challenge: Tell a first-time job seeker within seconds whether an offer, recruiter or posting is real.

title: The billing screen that freezes at the busiest hour
problem: Billing at Indian shop counters freezes during busy hours, settings reset after updates and bugs can take 3–4 months to fix, so invoices shared on WhatsApp arrive blank. Owners fall back to a paper khata for small credit because logging it while serving the next customer is too slow, and paper notes get lost. One supplier waited over 15 days for support, only to be told the shop's network was to blame.
challenge: Let a shopkeeper record a sale or a credit entry in under 5 seconds, even with no network.

title: Small tweaks and AI hours that never get billed
problem: Freelancers and small agencies leak margin through unbilled client tweaks, retainer hours nobody tracks, and time spent prompting and waiting on AI that no timesheet captures. Larger projects get underpriced at the start, and firms that pay in parts see freelancers disappear midway with money paid and work unfinished.
challenge: Show a freelancer, every week, exactly which unbilled work is eating their margin and what to charge for it.

title: The empty box that comes back as a return
problem: Small Meesho fashion sellers find 5–12% of returns come back as wrong or tampered items, and some as empty boxes. Claims must be filed within 48–72 hours with heavy photo proof, under a quarter succeed without proof of packing, and one reseller's account was suspended for appealing. Buyers face the mirror image: 3 lipsticks missing from a sealed Nykaa order, and no way to prove it.
challenge: Give a small seller proof of what went into every parcel that a marketplace will actually accept.

title: Milk poured daily, incentives paid 4 months late
problem: Nearly 4 lakh farmers who supply Aavin in Tamil Nadu went 4 months without their per-litre incentives, while village societies ran at a loss. Dairy farmers in Kenya's Rift Valley were owed 4 months of milk payments and could not cover feed or school fees. Collectives short of working capital cannot say when members will be paid, so farmers drift to private buyers.
challenge: Make sure every dairy farmer knows, each evening, what they are owed and when it will arrive.

title: The food reel paid for with a free meal
problem: Micro food bloggers in India are often paid only in free meals, with no standard rates or agreed deliverables, so their income is unpredictable. Restaurants cannot spot inflated follower counts or tell whether a reel brought in a single paying diner, so they will not pay real money. Small food brands are just as lost on ads, unable to tell paid demand from organic while spend returns barely 1.2–1.5x.
challenge: Let a small food creator prove what their last reel sold, and get paid for it.

title: FASTag tolls for a truck that was parked
problem: Small family truck operators move most of India's freight, and their earnings per trip are shrinking as costs rise. Several FASTag toll deductions hit one owner's truck while it was parked, and the refund was rejected. Another paid BlackBuck for access to loads, then got no loads for a month and no money back, while others find autopay charges taken without clear consent.
challenge: Catch every wrong toll, autopay and fee on a truck owner's account, and get it refunded.

title: The memory slip you can't hear over the phone
problem: Children living far from an ageing parent struggle to notice a slow decline in memory from ordinary phone calls. The internet is dangerous for an elder whose judgement is slipping, yet daily life is nearly impossible without it, and digital payment scams aimed at elders have risen sharply. Y Combinator's 2026 call for startups put it plainly: almost no technology is built for older people.
challenge: Help a family notice a parent's memory slipping early, and keep that parent safe online meanwhile.

title: The bus that never arrives, and nobody tells you
problem: Intercity buses are cancelled the day before travel, or never reach the boarding point at all, and no one warns the passenger. They find out at the roadside, with no other bus offered and no word on their refund. The same story turns up in reports from December 2025, June 2026 and October 2026.
challenge: Get a stranded passenger onto the next bus before they've left the stop.

title: Suspended overnight and never told why
problem: Indian creators lose channels and seller accounts overnight for policy breaches nobody names, sometimes over a linked account they cannot even identify. Appeals vanish without a reply, so a business built over years stops earning with no way to fix the actual problem.
challenge: Turn a vague suspension notice into a clear, evidence-backed appeal filed in one afternoon.

title: Weeks of setup, then a gateway rejection nobody explains
problem: Small businesses spend weeks integrating a payment gateway, then get rejected for their line of business with no clear reason, or turned down by a machine check with no human review and no refund of the onboarding fee. One waited over a month for activation, unable to take payments online. Live accounts are not safe either: one was closed for suspicious patterns its own upsell checkout created, and another had payouts frozen for months.
challenge: Get a small business approved to take payments online at the first attempt.

title: A paid listing, hundreds of hits, no real tenant
problem: Landlords on paid listing plans see hundreds of hits and not a single genuine tenant enquiry. In June 2026 an owner who bought a MagicBricks premium plan got no genuine tenant or buyer enquiries, and a long-time landlord says leads from TenantCloud have deteriorated badly. The landlord pays twice: once for the plan, and again in time lost on calls that go nowhere.
challenge: Sort a landlord's rental enquiries into real tenants and noise before anyone picks up the phone.

title: Good marks, but can't fix a bug
problem: Most engineering and MBA graduates of 2026 are still unplaced, and those from campuses few recruiters visit are far less likely to be hired. Employers say fresh graduates with good marks cannot debug code or apply what they learnt, because colleges teach mostly theory. Most students believe they are ready for work, few employers agree, and firms want ready hires without paying to train them.
challenge: Let a graduate from a small college prove one real skill to an employer in a single afternoon.

title: 2 lakh kiranas closed in a single year
problem: A retailer federation says 2 lakh kiranas closed in a year, and 60% of Mumbai grocery stores near quick-commerce dark stores saw volumes fall. Buying through distributors and stocking only 1,000–1,500 items, a kirana cannot match dark-store prices or range. It needs hundreds of loyal households to survive on thin margins, so a handful of defections can be enough to close it.
challenge: Help a kirana keep its loyal households ordering from it rather than from the nearest dark store.

title: 150 applications, 2 interviews, and not one reason why
problem: Experienced people apply steadily, some for over a year, and hear nothing back. One job seeker sent around 150 applications and got 2 interviews. Hiring filters never show what they read or why they said no, so people guess at length, format and how to explain a career break, and burn out guessing.
challenge: Tell a job seeker, with evidence, why their applications stall and the one change to make next.

title: A confirmed salon slot, and still a half-hour wait
problem: Indian salons lose 4–5 appointments a day to no-shows, over ₹70,000 a month. Customers who do turn up with a confirmed slot still wait half an hour, because bookings are kept by hand and ignore how long each service takes. When a stylist is out, every affected client has to be called one by one.
challenge: Cut a salon's no-shows and waiting time in half without adding a receptionist.

title: Crops ploughed under because the mandi offered ₹2
problem: Small growers of onion, tomato, gourd, coconut and grains sell into the one market and the few traders within reach, often at ₹2 to ₹8 a kilo when it cost more to grow. Prices swing by half within days and nobody tells a grower where a better buyer sits a few hours away, so whole harvests are dumped or ploughed back into the soil.
challenge: Tell a small grower, before harvest day, where and when their crop will fetch the most.

title: One viral reel and the home bakery breaks
problem: Home chefs struggle with reliable delivery, spill-proof packaging and steady quality, and a single viral post can flood a small food seller with more orders than its stock and hands can manage. Customised celebration cakes arrive hours late or damaged, ruining birthdays, and the seller's reputation takes the hit.
challenge: Help a home food seller say yes to the right number of orders and deliver every one intact.

title: The carrier who collects the load, then vanishes
problem: Hundreds of carriers and brokers can register at a single mailbox address, and carrier numbers are cheap, so a shipper cannot tell a real carrier from an impostor. Cargo theft through spoofed identities rose sharply in 2025 and 2026, faster than the manual checks brokers rely on. Brokers are still liable for poor vetting, with no quick way to check who they are handing a load to.
challenge: Tell a shipper within a minute whether the carrier on the phone is who they claim to be.

title: The meal nobody logs, and the coach advising blind
problem: Online nutrition coaches advise from their clients' food logs, but typing every meal is tedious and logs from separate trackers sync unreliably, so coaches see half the picture. Clients would rather send a photo of the plate, and when the coach's reply comes late, the weight creeps back. Coaches have posted the same complaint in reviews from May 2025 to September 2026.
challenge: Let a client log a whole day of meals in under a minute, and the coach see it the same day.

title: Paid in full, and the hotel has no record
problem: Travellers arrive with a paid voucher and a confirmation to find the hotel has no record of them, no room, or the wrong number of guests. Booking sites and hotel inventory drift out of sync, and in August 2026 a corporate booking for 4 guests was recorded as 1, forcing a large surcharge at the desk. The traveller pays twice or sleeps elsewhere.
challenge: Make sure the hotel knows about a paid booking, with the right guests, before the traveller arrives.

title: Labelled AI-made, and the creator cannot take it off
problem: Automatic labels for synthetic media rolled out across the major video services in 2025, and they catch genuine work: in October 2026 a creator's green-screen video was tagged as AI-generated and the label locked. Crackdowns on machine-made content now bury faceless creators however much effort they put in, while a fully synthetic influencer gathered millions of followers who believed she was real.
challenge: Let a creator prove a piece of work is theirs and human-made, in a way any viewer can check in seconds.

title: The claim rejected over a clause nobody explained
problem: Over half of Indian health insurance claimants face rejection or partial approval, often over exclusions buried in legal language or paperwork they did not understand. Premiums have jumped 50–200% in 3 years, and hospital discharge waits stretch to 2 days. Families then fight the insurer through the ombudsman alone.
challenge: Help a family get a health claim paid in full on the first submission.

title: Paid for inspections, and nobody ever came
problem: Landlords pay for property management or tenant-finding, then get no showings, no inspections and a manager who goes silent, and refunds are refused. One owner paying NoBroker a percentage fee in October 2026 got no inspections, missing tenant documents and no lease enforcement. Owners in other cities or abroad find out only when something has already gone wrong.
challenge: Give a distant landlord proof, every month, that someone visited and checked their flat.

title: Paid for the course, then the company went silent
problem: Learners pay for courses, books, certificates and exam help, and then the books never arrive, the certificate stays locked or the classes freeze right before exams. One online degree provider took a ₹10,000 reservation fee, rejected the applicant and kept the money. Refunds are denied over terms the buyer never clearly saw, and follow-ups go unanswered until the buyer stops chasing.
challenge: Get a stranded learner their money back, or a written answer, within 2 weeks of the first complaint.

title: Fake cash-on-delivery orders bleeding small sellers
problem: Small online sellers lose around ₹600 on every fake or refused cash-on-delivery order once shipping and ad spend are counted, and competitors place bomb orders on purpose. The verification add-ons meant to catch them break for days, while scammers send unordered cash-on-delivery parcels to leaked addresses under real stores' names.
challenge: Stop fake cash-on-delivery orders before they ship, without turning away real first-time buyers.

title: Sold on the demo, still not live months later
problem: Mid-size firms buy HR and payroll packages on the strength of a demo, then find limits the demo hid and an implementation team that stops replying. One company was still not live 2.5 months after buying, with no manuals, and configuring approvals and forms in-house is slow. Staff come to hate what they paid for, and a refund promised during the sale never arrived.
challenge: Get a mid-size firm live on new HR and payroll in 2 weeks, with every approval flow tested first.

title: Bridal slots booked in DMs, lost to ghosting
problem: Freelance makeup artists, mehendi artists and saree drapers take bookings through direct messages with no deposit, contract or trial, so one ghosted wedding slot wipes out a full day's income. Customers face the mirror image: no way to find a skilled freelancer at short notice, and nothing to fall back on when a ₹2 lakh look goes wrong.
challenge: Make booking a freelance beauty professional as binding as booking a salon, with a deposit, a trial and a findable profile.

title: Growers get ₹5–7 a kilo, kitchens pay retail
problem: Onion and potato growers get barely 43% of the retail price, and mandi rates have crashed to ₹5–7 a kilo while shoppers still pay high. Independent restaurants nearby pay retail for the same produce, because wholesalers want minimum orders bigger than they can store. Growers who try to sell direct end up building their own farm-to-plate network just to get paid fairly and on time.
challenge: Connect small growers to the kitchens near them, with orders sized for both and paid within the week.

title: Card money that never reaches the restaurant
problem: Restaurants run on same-day cash for suppliers and wages, yet card settlements arrive late, and after a change of bank details some stop arriving at all while support cannot trace them. Refunds owed by vendors after a cancelled contract can vanish the same way, squeezing working capital in a business with thin margins.
challenge: Tell a restaurant owner every morning which payments are due, which are late, and who to chase.

title: Every small export order carries a big exporter's paperwork
problem: Low-value shipments make up a large share of India's shipping bills, yet small exporters carry the same paperwork, and the same chasing of bank proof that the money arrived, as the biggest. Matching many small export receipts to bank entries is slow, and labelling rules reported in September 2026 add proof that materials are free of toxic substances to every shipment.
challenge: Close every small export's paperwork and bank entries within a week of payment, without a full-time clerk.

title: Booked, travelled, and the doctor is on leave
problem: Patients book a specialist online, travel to the appointment and find the doctor on leave, not practising at that hospital, or the clinic shut, with no warning from anyone. The fee shown online can be half what the clinic charges at the visit. Reports like these run from November 2025 to August 2026, and support lines rarely confirm anything before the trip.
challenge: Make sure a patient who books a doctor finds that doctor, at that place, at that price.

title: The fare you only learn when the ride ends
problem: In a 2025 survey, 59% of ride-hailing riders faced charges added only at the end of the trip, and one rider paid about 4 times the estimated fare for the same route. Riders who get out early are still billed to the final destination. In Bengaluru, auto fares on ride services have crept above the meter rate since subsidies ended.
challenge: Tell a rider before booking what this trip should cost, and flag the overcharge before they pay.

title: Brand money stops at the metro limits
problem: 2 in 3 Indian creators come from smaller cities, and regional-language creators now outnumber the rest, yet brand spend still flows mostly to metro creators. Most land only 1 paid campaign a year, so creating rarely becomes an income. Affiliate networks are cluttered and assume an agency, which shuts small creators out of the other way to earn.
challenge: Help a small-town creator land their second paid campaign this quarter, not next year.

title: Scammed over UPI, and the money never comes back
problem: 1 in 5 Indian families that use UPI has been hit by fraud in 3 years, and half of victims never complained because reporting felt pointless or complicated. Fraud is roughly doubling every year, while victims recover only a small fraction. Fake merchants and lenders that are not RBI-registered operate freely, and payment gateways have refused to investigate.
challenge: Get a scam victim's complaint filed everywhere it matters within the first hour.

title: Wiring a deposit to someone who cloned the listing
problem: Scammers clone real rental listings, impersonate the owner and collect deposits for homes that are not for rent, and police have logged hundreds of such reports. Renters who toured a real flat still wire money to the wrong person, and students lose PG booking deposits to owners who vanish. A deposit is often a month or more of savings.
challenge: Let a renter confirm, before sending any money, that the person asking for it really controls the home.

title: Patient one-on-one tutoring is still for the few
problem: Most young children learn reading and arithmetic without patient one-on-one help, because tutoring that adapts to each child is reserved for the few. Parents want to let children explore an encyclopedia or AI assistant on their own, but have no child-safe controls over what it says, and struggle to explain where AI fails. Parents were asking for those controls as early as May 2025, and the worry is now mainstream.
challenge: Give a young child a patient voice tutor whose every answer a parent can limit and review.

title: Your own business records, held hostage by the vendor
problem: Small firms depend on vendors and implementation partners to reach their own records: in November 2025 a partner deleted a company's Odoo database without permission. Vendors break upgrade promises and change renewal terms at will, and some families keep 1980s business software alive in emulators because moving the data feels impossible.
challenge: Get a small business's records out of any old setup into a file it owns, in an afternoon.

title: Every HR change waits for the one admin
problem: HR setups are so complex that staff wait while someone works through every feature, and routine workflows and reports still need an admin to step in. Every role sees the same crowded screens, so workarounds pile up until the setup makes more work than it saves. HR managers, recruiters and analysts have said so in reviews from April to September 2026.
challenge: Let any manager change an HR workflow or pull a report by describing it in one sentence, without the admin.

title: The foundation shade that turns wrong by noon
problem: Indian buyers often order several wrong foundation shades online, because undertone and oxidation do not show in a product photo and the shade turns wrong within hours. Bridal artists often apply one standard look to darker skin, and imported skincare made for cooler climates irritates in Indian humidity and pollution. Every wrong bottle is money spent on something that was never going to suit.
challenge: Help someone find a shade and a routine that work on their skin before they spend a rupee.

title: Pest advice that arrives after the crop is gone
problem: Farmers struggle to get timely crop and cattle advice in their own language, so a vet visit costs money and days while informal advice often misleads. Pest attacks arrive without early warning, sprays are applied by guesswork, and residues end up in food while pests adapt.
challenge: Give a farmer a trustworthy answer about a sick plant or animal, in their language, within the hour.

title: Every rupee of the menu price already spoken for
problem: Owner-run restaurants were hit by rising ingredient, labour and rent costs in 2025, on top of taxes, card fees and aggregator commissions. Card fees alone push owners to raise menu prices or add surcharges that irritate diners. Chains and fast-food stands ride out the squeeze while owner-run places buckle.
challenge: Show a restaurant owner, dish by dish, where the money goes and which change would save the most this month.

title: The shipping wallet that eats a seller's cash
problem: Small online sellers prepay shipping into a courier aggregator's wallet and wait on cash-on-delivery remittances, then watch unexplained deductions, disputed weight charges and add-ons eat into that money. Shiprocket sellers reported debits support could not explain or reverse in October 2025, and in July 2026 a frozen wallet blocked one seller's dispatches entirely.
challenge: Show a small seller every rupee the courier holds or took, and get the wrong ones back within a week.

title: A hospital bill with nothing to check it against
problem: Patients get long itemised hospital bills with no upfront price for a routine procedure to compare against, and the same visit can cost far more depending on how it is coded. People without health cover pay the highest rates, and medical bills push families into debt. Courts and regulators pushed Indian hospitals to publish standard rates in 2024 and 2025, yet the bill still arrives before any price does.
challenge: Tell a patient before admission what a routine procedure should cost, and flag what does not belong on the bill.

title: Drivers cancel the moment they see your destination
problem: In a 2026 survey, 82% of ride-hailing riders had faced driver cancellations, often after the driver learned the destination or that they would pay digitally. Airport bookings get stuck in accept-then-cancel loops, and one rider waited over 20 minutes for a driver who then refused the trip. A missed early-morning airport ride costs far more than the small credit given back.
challenge: Get a rider to the airport on time even when 3 drivers cancel in a row.

title: The influencer budget nobody can prove paid off
problem: 2 in 5 brands say they cannot measure return on influencer campaigns, and judging them on direct-response numbers misses the trust they build. Agencies spend hours every week exporting ad data, cleaning it and building client reports in spreadsheets. Budget meetings still end on the same question: did it work?
challenge: Show a brand what each creator campaign returned, in a report nobody has to build by hand.

title: Paid in 90 days, paying their vendors in 30
problem: Small suppliers wait 60–90 days or more for big buyers to pay, while paying their own vendors in 30, and borrow at high interest to bridge the gap. Wages, raw material and loan repayments get squeezed, and one supplier spent 6 months chasing a single delayed payment. The 45-day rule meant to protect them has some buyers avoiding registered small suppliers altogether.
challenge: Shorten the gap between delivery and payment for a small supplier by a month.

title: The quote that grows once the advance is paid
problem: Painting and interior jobs start with a low quote that balloons with extras once work begins, and the quotations are too confusing to push back on. In September 2026 one interiors firm took a ₹1 lakh advance, then quoted many times the original estimate and refused a refund. Another painting job was billed near ₹2 lakh, with substandard work and the wrong materials installed.
challenge: Turn any interiors or painting quote into a fair-price check a homeowner can take back to the contractor the same day.

title: 100 applications, 7 interviews, and no feedback
problem: One candidate got interviews from just 7 of 100 applications, and new graduates in a weak junior market hear almost nothing back. Keyword filters reject qualified freshers for missing a brand name, ghost listings waste their time and boards are flooded with machine-written applications. Candidates lose track of where they applied, submit twice, miss follow-ups and get ghosted after long interview rounds.
challenge: Turn a graduate's next 50 applications into 20 targeted ones that each get a reply.

title: Same van, same costs, 50 shops instead of 80
problem: Metro consumer-goods distributors are losing 10–25% of snack and beverage volume to quick commerce, and revenue per kirana stop has dropped 15–30%. Their vans now serve 50 kiranas instead of 80 while costs stay fixed. Struggling shops then pay late, stretching 30–60 day credit further, so the distributor is squeezed from both sides.
challenge: Help a distributor win back revenue per route, or cut the cost of serving each shop, by a fifth.

title: The sync that broke 3 payroll cycles ago
problem: Payment notifications that never arrive, scheduled jobs that report success while doing nothing, and backups that never covered a critical store all fail without an alarm, and teams find out hours later if at all. One healthcare HR team keyed in leave by hand for 61 staff across 3 payroll cycles because a time-clock sync had quietly broken.
challenge: Tell a small team within the hour when data that should have moved between their services did not.

title: Bought from the official store, delivered as a fake
problem: 40% of Indian cosmetics buyers have hit counterfeits in 3 years, with online platforms the top source, and a quarter of them reported allergic reactions. Commingled inventory means even a brand's official storefront can ship a fake, and a Meesho Mall order in June 2026 arrived old, used and in worn packaging. Every fake makes buyers trust every seller a little less.
challenge: Show a beauty buyer where a specific unit came from before it touches their skin.

title: Fruit that rots between the field and the buyer
problem: Up to 15 percent of fruit and 12 percent of vegetables are lost between harvest and sale, because growers lack storage and grading at the farm gate and sell into gluts. Perishable shipments that do move are delayed or damaged in transit with no record of what happened, so claims go nowhere.
challenge: Make it cheaper for a grower to hold, grade or ship a perishable crop than to dump it.

title: Too big for retail, too small for wholesale
problem: Small restaurants pay suppliers more because their orders are unpredictable, and vendors discount only for committed, prepaid volumes. Large joint families buying staples in bulk still pay consumer prices, because grocery services sell only retail packs. For an owner who works 14-hour shifts and keeps almost nothing once ingredients, wages and rent are paid, that premium hurt more after the food inflation of 2025.
challenge: Get a small kitchen or a big household wholesale prices without prepaying for a truckload.

title: Broken in transit, and the claim takes forever
problem: Online sellers lose or see damaged a few percent of parcels in transit, and fragile goods suffer most because handling instructions are ignored. Claims drag on for weeks, insurance claims get denied for lack of evidence, and the seller usually absorbs the loss.
challenge: Get a seller paid for a broken or lost parcel in days, not weeks.

title: Wrong medicine at the door, and the return refused
problem: Medicines arrive with expiry dates washed off, vaccines arrive at room temperature, and a wrong drug is refused for return because the buyer supposedly checked it on delivery. Complaints sit unresolved for months. India's top 300 drug brands have carried QR codes since 2023, yet a patient holding a strip still cannot tell if it is right, in date and genuine.
challenge: Let a patient know, before accepting a delivery, that a medicine is the right drug, in date and genuine.

title: Airline refunded weeks ago, and the money never arrived
problem: Airlines release refunds for cancelled flights to online travel agents, who sit on them for weeks before anything reaches the traveller, even on fares paid in full up front. When one leg of a connecting flight is cancelled, the refund for the whole one-way ticket can go missing. Train passengers delayed 3 hours or more see refund claims rejected on technicalities.
challenge: Get every refund a traveller is owed into their account without them writing a single email.

title: Lakhs owed, and the brand pays when it likes
problem: Indian creators routinely wait over 2 months for brands to pay, and small agencies have dues outstanding for over a year, far past the 90-day cycle. Creators under half a million followers negotiate, invoice and chase alone, so many now refuse new work without a 25–50% advance. The problem is so common that one agency pays creators from its own balance sheet.
challenge: Get a creator paid on time for brand work without a single awkward reminder.

title: Foreign client paid, freelancer still waiting
problem: Freelancers and small sellers earning from abroad see payouts held for days, accounts blocked over address typos or missed OTPs, and funds returned to clients without clear reason. Surprise fees and poor conversion routes shave off more, and some clients never pay what they promised.
challenge: Get an Indian freelancer's foreign earnings into their bank on a predictable day, at a known cost.

title: Paying an inspection fee to hear an inflated quote
problem: Appliance technicians charge an inspection fee, then push part replacements nobody can check, at inflated prices. Air conditioner installation costs vary several-fold for the same job, with surprise extras for piping and brackets. In September 2026, an AC repair booked through Urban Company was allegedly misdiagnosed and sold with the wrong warranty information.
challenge: Give a household a second opinion on a repair quote before they say yes to the technician.

title: ₹2.5 lakh on a data course, and zero interviews
problem: Learners pay lakhs for tech and data courses sold with placement guarantees, then meet weak teaching, labs that barely work and support that goes silent. One paid about ₹2.5 lakh and had zero interviews 3 months after finishing; another spent 1.6 years and ₹3 lakh and is still unplaced. They lose the fee, the time and the job they were promised.
challenge: Show a learner, before they pay, what the last batch of a course actually went on to do.

title: Sold out of fast sellers, stuck with slow ones
problem: Kirana owners reorder hundreds of items by gut feel, running out of fast sellers while slow stock ties up cash. They stock what distributors push rather than what shoppers ask for, so customers settle for second-best or come back tomorrow. Small shops live on turning stock: one independent bookshop has to turn its shelves 4–5 times a year just to cover fixed costs.
challenge: Make the weekly reorder take 10 minutes and leave fewer empty shelves and fewer dusty ones.

title: The support ticket that holds up everyone's salary
problem: Small teams get support requests across chat servers, code trackers and email with no single place to see them, so urgent ones wait behind trivial ones. Customers who phone sit through long holds and phone trees. A query stuck with an HR provider's support during payroll week can stop salaries going out.
challenge: Answer a small team's routine support questions in minutes, and get the urgent ones to a person first.

title: The lipstick arrived opened, and the return was refused
problem: Beauty and grocery buyers cannot see a manufacturing or best-before date before ordering, so skincare has arrived with 13 of its 24 months of shelf life already gone. When a perfume came with a tampered seal, Nykaa refused the return; Purplle did the same for a used lipstick. The buyer is left unsure whether they got something used, fake or old.
challenge: Make a beauty order's shelf life and seal visible before payment, and provable after delivery.

title: The farm ledger nobody finishes setting up
problem: Farm accounting packages want entities and a chart of accounts configured before they do anything useful, record entry is tedious, and input stock does not update when a purchase is logged. Bank reconciliation is slow, so the books fall behind. In September 2026, women-led farmer producer companies were reported folding once grants ended, lacking management skills and financial literacy.
challenge: Turn a farm's receipts and purchases into usable books on the first day, with no setup.

title: The restaurant that can't call its own regulars
problem: Delivery aggregators mask customer details, so a restaurant cannot build a direct relationship with the people who order from it. In 2025 aggregators launched their own food brands, and restaurants fear the order data they generate will be used to compete with them. Small owners lack the time to keep a website current, so every repeat order still goes through the aggregator.
challenge: Help a small restaurant turn one-time delivery customers into regulars who order direct.

title: Pickup today, says the message, every day
problem: Small sellers get repeated pickup-scheduled messages while no courier arrives, so dispatch slips for days and buyers get angry. Prepaid shipping is not refunded, dashboards make rescheduling hard, and some shipments show no movement for weeks.
challenge: Make sure a booked pickup happens the same day, or a different courier comes.

title: The claim rejected, and nobody will say why
problem: Over 40% of surveyed Indian policyholders say health claims were rejected or only part paid for reasons they consider invalid, and nobody explains the decision. Half of those filing cashless claims waited 6–48 hours for approval before discharge, even after IRDAI tightened cashless timelines in 2024.
challenge: Help a family fight a rejected health claim with the right clause and the right letter, in one evening.

title: The bus moved and nobody told the passenger
problem: Intercity buses change pickup points by phone, run hours late or leave while booked passengers are minutes away. Live tracking and driver contact numbers are often wrong, so passengers miss buses and lose the fare.
challenge: Make sure every passenger knows where and when their bus really is, before they leave home.

title: The blog worth reading that search no longer shows
problem: Independent blogs and niche forums have become hard to find through mainstream search, and since AI answers began replacing clicks in 2025, staying visible takes a huge content effort with uncertain returns. As synthetic content floods feeds, readers trust less of what they see, and human writers get buried beneath it.
challenge: Get a small independent writer found by the readers already searching for exactly what they write.

title: The fees on your statement you never agreed to
problem: Indian cardholders unknowingly pay thousands of crores in surprise annual fees, late fees and add-ons buried in their statements, and most bank customers cannot easily spot or reverse them. A 2.5% surcharge can appear at a wallet checkout with no warning, and trading fees arrive with no breakdown of what was charged or why.
challenge: Find every fee a household paid this year that it could have avoided, and get it reversed.

title: Paid to avoid brokers, and still calling brokers
problem: Renters pay for owner-only plans and still get handed broker numbers, as one paying house hunter reported in September 2026. Many attractive listings are broker bait, with borrowed photos or homes that are not available. Support goes quiet once the subscription is sold, and relationship managers change so often that nobody owns the promise made at sale.
challenge: Flag a broker posing as an owner, or a borrowed photo, before a renter makes the call.

title: College advice paid for by the colleges
problem: School leavers in India get college advice from counsellors who earn referral commissions, steering them toward costly private colleges. Young people leaving formal education lack mentors and structure, and teenagers who can already code cannot find paid internships to test a direction. A wrong choice at eighteen costs years and lakhs of rupees.
challenge: Give a school leaver advice on what to study next that no college has paid to influence.

title: Card fees and add-ons eating a shop's margin
problem: Small retailers pay flat processing fees plus a monthly charge for nearly every point-of-sale feature, and surprise invoices for using an outside card processor. One shop spends about $400 a month on card fees, chargebacks go through without goods returned, and basic stock valuation reports cost extra.
challenge: Show a small retailer exactly what payments and software cost per sale, and how to cut it.

title: The answer is in someone's head, and they're away
problem: Team know-how sits in a few heads and in old email, chat threads and tickets, and internal wikis decay because writing things down is tedious. Newcomers depend on whoever happens to know, search finds nothing useful, and work stalls when that person is away. Threads from April 2025 to April 2026 keep reaching the same finding: documentation never catches up unless capture happens on its own.
challenge: Keep a team's know-how written down as a side effect of the work it already does, with nobody editing a wiki.

title: A quarter of a shopkeeper's wage, for handwoven cloth
problem: A March 2025 report found Indian handloom weavers earn a quarter of what shopkeepers do, losing margin to middlemen and powerloom copies. They sell through seasonal fairs at prices that barely cover costs, and selling online means website builders that assume design and technical skills they do not have.
challenge: Let a weaver list a piece for sale online from a phone, in their own language, in 5 minutes.

title: Signed up for carbon credits, and never paid
problem: Farmers in private carbon programmes do not know what they will earn or when, see payouts cut without explanation, and never get back the soil test results taken from their own fields. A December 2024 study found nearly all farmers in voluntary carbon projects received no payment, and over a quarter quit. The company apps meant to keep them informed go ignored.
challenge: Show every enrolled farmer what their fields have earned, why, and when the money arrives.

title: 6 fees stacked on top of one meal
problem: One delivery receipt in September 2026 stacked 6 separate fees on top of the food, making the real price impossible to judge before checkout. Delivery services raised fees several times within weeks in 2025 and moved to pass new GST on delivery fees to customers, so the same meal can cost nearly double what the restaurant's own site charges. Some riders still demand extra cash on top.
challenge: Show a hungry customer the true total for the same order across every way of buying it, before they pay.

title: The idle truck nobody puts a price on
problem: Indian fleet owners face rising operating costs, yet vehicle downtime, one of their largest hidden expenses, is rarely tracked or planned for. Fleetio's promised telematics sync did not reliably fill in vehicle data, so records still needed manual cleanup, and a 2026 interface update forced one fleet team to retrain the staff who log inspections and repairs.
challenge: Show a fleet owner what each idle day costs in rupees, without anyone typing in more data.

title: The home exercises nobody does once sessions end
problem: Patients and coaching clients tend to stop their home exercises once paid sessions end, and coaches cannot compare what was prescribed with what was done. Exercise libraries skew young, so one coach for middle-aged women filmed many exercises herself, and older clients find remote programmes confusing. In July 2026 a client of a paid fitness coach got only forwarded YouTube videos, no follow-up, and regained the weight.
challenge: Show a coach which clients actually did this week's exercises, and how well, without a single extra call.

title: Airline refunded in full, traveller got ₹1,750 less
problem: Online travel agents keep their convenience fee even when the airline cancels, deduct coupon value from refunds without warning, and pass on less than the airline paid back. In one April 2026 case the airline refunded the agent in full and the traveller received about ₹1,750 less. Near-identical reschedules get different refund rules, so nobody knows what they are owed.
challenge: Show a traveller exactly what the airline refunded, and make sure every rupee of it reaches them.

title: Money stuck, and only a bot will answer
problem: Creator and payment services moved most of their support to bots in 2025, so when money goes wrong there is often no human to reach. One link-in-bio service kept taking payments a creator never authorised while its support bot said the account did not exist. In India, account managers change without notice once a subscription is paid, and unresponsive payment support has sunk an organiser's ticket sales.
challenge: Get a small seller's stuck money or broken account in front of a human who can fix it, within a day.

title: The GST notice: pay it, or reply to it?
problem: Small taxpayers receive GST demand notices without knowing whether to pay or reply, and guessing wrong risks penalties or an order passed without them being heard. As of July 2026, repeated e-way bill rule changes leave small businesses and their billing vendors unsure what to comply with and when. Getting it right still means reading dense rules and cross-checking documents by hand.
challenge: Tell a small business what a notice means, what to file and by when, in its own language, within the hour.

title: The token amount that never comes back
problem: Renters pay a token advance to hold a flat, then the owner backs out or rents it to someone else and the refund stays pending for months. Escalation contacts do not work and managers stop responding. Small sums vanish because chasing them costs more than they are worth.
challenge: Make a rental token refundable by default, released only when both sides confirm the deal.

title: A year of exam prep, paid upfront
problem: Exam-prep courses demand non-refundable yearly fees upfront, with no way to pay per topic or try first. Buyers find advertised content later locked behind a pricier tier, are pushed into instalment plans with threats about credit scores, and cannot move a paid batch when they switch streams. Students on tight budgets pay for a year they may never use.
challenge: Let an exam aspirant pay only for the topics and weeks they actually use.

title: One flag and a seller's balance is gone
problem: Small online sellers depend on a handful of marketplaces and payment providers that can close an account overnight and freeze its balance for months, sometimes after one unusually large sale. Honest market vendors have lost their main way to get paid because a provider banned every customer of one fraudulent stall.
challenge: Keep a small seller trading and paid on the day one marketplace or payment provider freezes them.

title: Decided in the chat, never on the task list
problem: Small teams split work across chat, task and document tools, so decisions made in a thread never reach the task list, and promises made aloud, like sending a file, are forgotten. In one 2025 case the official work chat failed and staff moved real discussions into personal WhatsApp groups, scattering decisions and leaking company information. People waiting on several colleagues lose track of who owes what, and for how long.
challenge: Turn every promise made in a chat or a call into a task with an owner and a date, the same day.

title: Hand-counted commissions, and the disputes that follow
problem: Indian salon owners spend over 10 hours a month on GST reconciliation and still work out commissions and attendance by hand, which keeps causing disputes with staff. Those who move to software like Zenoti have seen financial data mapped wrongly in migration, loyalty and membership rules too fiddly to set up, and only a support bot when billing breaks.
challenge: Make a salon's month-end close, commissions and GST included, take an hour and end with no staff disputes.

title: The watermelon nobody could trace
problem: When a family in Mumbai died after eating a contaminated watermelon, nobody could trace where it came from. Vegetables reaching Delhi through Azadpur carry no record of whether drain water grew them, and in July 2026 cakes ordered online arrived stale with no record of when they were made. Buyers cannot judge safety, and honest sellers cannot prove it.
challenge: Let a fruit seller or small food maker prove where and when their food was grown or made, for paise a label.

title: Infested kitchens, and diners order blind
problem: A September 2026 inspection drive in Hyderabad found infestations, expired stock and poor handler hygiene in most of the restaurants it checked. That same month, live insects turned up inside a sealed noodle packet bought through quick commerce. Diners ordering online still have no way to see a kitchen's hygiene before they pay.
challenge: Let a diner see how clean a kitchen is before ordering, in a way the kitchen cannot fake.

title: No paid seat, no way to log the fault
problem: A chemical plant could afford only a few full MaintainX seats, so everyone else logs maintenance work through someone who has one, and the data suffers. A machinery firm pays full licence price for staff who log a fault now and then, because there is no shared or low-usage seat. Most of this work happens away from a desk, yet software for maintenance crews has barely changed in 20 years.
challenge: Let anyone on the shop floor log a fault in 10 seconds, without a paid seat.

title: Clinics pay lakhs for listings that bring one patient
problem: Indian doctors pay booking marketplaces tens of thousands to lakhs a year for visibility and receive a handful of leads or none. Terms change without notice, ads stop running, and support vanishes after the sale, while the middlemen take a growing share of what patients pay.
challenge: Show a small clinic exactly which rupee of its marketing brought which patient.

title: The flexible fare that wasn't, and a no-show instead
problem: Flexible fares, free-cancellation add-ons, travel insurance and baggage allowances are sold at checkout and then not honoured: a flexi-fare booking was marked no-show instead of changed, insurance covered the wrong dates, and a promised bag was missing from the ticket. India's dark-pattern guidelines named pre-ticked add-ons and travel agents were asked to audit them in 2025, yet the complaints kept coming through 2026.
challenge: Tell a traveller, before they pay, exactly what each add-on will and will not cover.

title: 11 weeks in monetisation review, and nobody to ask
problem: Creators who cross the monetisation thresholds can wait months in review: one has waited over 11 weeks for a re-review with no timeline from support. A viral Short with millions of views can be left out of the eligibility count with no reason given, and the earnings page in YouTube Studio lags by days. So creators keep uploading blind while income they qualified for stays out of reach.
challenge: Tell a creator where their monetisation stands and what to fix next, in plain words, in under a minute.

title: Prising ledgers out of Tally piece by piece
problem: Accountants pull ledgers out of TallyPrime piece by piece to analyse them, which is slow and lets errors creep into their reports. Elsewhere, a bookkeeper can bulk-update only 25 items at a time and has no project cost reports, so hours go on repetitive edits. The rest of the day goes on switching between full-screen spreadsheets.
challenge: Get every ledger out of Tally in one clean pull, ready to analyse in minutes rather than a day.

title: 6 months' rent upfront, and cuts nobody explains
problem: Bengaluru brokers quote legal deposit limits that do not exist and still demand 6 months of rent upfront. At move-out, inspection teams inflate repair costs, and co-living operators cut flat amounts for service charges they never explain. Tenants lose money they have no way to contest, and new cases surfaced in both August and September 2026.
challenge: Give a tenant a deposit statement they can contest line by line before they hand back the keys.

title: Parents pay the tutor and never see the learning
problem: Parents pay for tuition and get no proof their child is learning, while tutors who solve the homework for them leave children weak in fundamentals. A tutoring business cannot move easily between attendance, notes and lesson plans, and has nowhere to share a report card per student. In September 2026 one parent paying for online coding and maths classes reported connectivity trouble and no visible progress at all.
challenge: Let a tutor show every parent what their child learnt this week, in the time it takes to pack up.

title: Over-order and block cash, or run out of stock
problem: Shop owners cannot see what their suppliers have in stock, so they either over-order and block cash or run out, and a main supplier's website search is often useless. Buying direct from brands is out of reach at small order sizes, so distributors take a large share of the margin. In August 2024 a retailer who bought rice wholesale online got poor-quality stock and had the return rejected.
challenge: Let a shopkeeper know what will arrive, and at what price, before the money leaves their hand.

title: Your fingers are the slowest part of the job
problem: Much of a working day now goes on writing messages and prompts, and for people who chat with AI heavily, typing speed has become the limit, worst of all for those who cannot type fast for long. Time away from the keyboard, like the drive to work, is lost, even though email could be triaged and replies drafted by voice. The complaint turned up in January 2025, May 2025 and January 2026.
challenge: Let someone clear their inbox and draft every reply by voice before they reach the office.

title: Years of size charts you cannot take with you
problem: Small clothing stores on Shopify pay per-order fees for size-chart add-ons, so fit guidance costs more as sales grow, and one merchant could not export years of charts they had built. Size recommenders stop working silently and the store finds out later, while a model's height and size or a virtual try-on is too crude for shoppers to trust. So returns stay high.
challenge: Give a small clothing store fit guidance it owns, that never silently breaks and costs nothing per order.

title: Queueing for urea, then paying above the subsidised price
problem: Farmers in Telangana queue for urea with no reliable word on which dealer has stock, then pay above the subsidised price and get pushed into tie-in purchases. Feed is no easier: poultry farmers have seen feed cost per egg nearly double and absorb about 20% losses, and nearly 3 in 4 small cattle rearers struggle to get affordable fodder. Buy inputs online instead, and a refund on AgroStar can go unanswered.
challenge: Show a farmer which dealer has urea today, at the fair price, before they leave home.

title: Spices, water and milk nobody can vouch for
problem: Families distrust packaged spice powders for adulteration and staleness, yet grinding fresh at home takes effort. They cannot tell whether a 20-litre water can is truly purified, or find the fat content of packaged milk and whether powder went into it. Every claim on the label has to be taken on trust, every day.
challenge: Help a family check its spices, water and milk at home in under 5 minutes.

title: Decades-old code, and nobody left who can fix it
problem: Small family businesses depend on custom code written decades ago that nobody left can repair, and as late as 2025 freight, travel and banking firms still ran on old terminal systems with modern screens layered on top. Heavily customised Odoo installs grow expensive to maintain, and every major upgrade threatens costly redevelopment and testing. Owners also fear losing access to their own books, with no good offline alternative.
challenge: Get a small firm off its old custom code, books intact, without stopping the business for a day.

title: Therapists write reports in the hours they should rest
problem: An autism services worker writes very long insurance justification reports every 6 months, with almost no time set aside for them. Staff at mid-sized Indian clinics spend about 11 hours a week on confirmation calls, copying paper into records, sending lab results and reconciling bills. It lands on people who are already overworked and underpaid.
challenge: Turn a therapist's session notes into a progress report ready to send before the next session starts.

title: Peer car rental runs on trust nobody can check
problem: Self-drive renters are blacklisted without reason or appeal, verification stalls before trips, listings use fake registration numbers, and hosts fail to hand over cars. Deposits and damage refunds stay pending for months.
challenge: Let a renter and a car owner verify each other and settle deposits without a third party.

title: Payout dates that move without a reason
problem: Expected payout dates slip by a full month, paid subscriber revenue fails to arrive, and Indian sellers wait on delayed payouts or see an account suspended the day before money is due, all without a reason shown. Creators who budget around these payments cannot plan rent, equipment or the next shoot.
challenge: Show every creator when each rupee they have earned will land, and raise the alarm the day it slips.

title: Ticking bank lines against the ledger, one by one
problem: Bookkeeping is repetitive and easy to check against the bank, yet small firms still reconcile their ledgers by hand, and it remains the slowest part of the work. The bank feeds meant to help keep dropping: in September 2026 one firm found transactions missing and support unable to fix the connection.
challenge: Match a small firm's month of bank lines to its ledger, leaving a person only the ones that need judgement.

title: Proving what was damaged and what it was worth
problem: When a technician damages an air conditioner compressor or a repair visit floods the home, households find no compensation process and service providers deny cover. Homeowners facing insurance claims must photograph and value every possession, a tedious job taking many hours. Without proof of what existed and what it cost, claims are cut or refused.
challenge: Help a household build a valued, photographed inventory of its home in under an hour.

title: Stuck on one problem with no one to ask
problem: Coaching students say only a few learners ever get live doubt sessions despite repeated requests, and offline centres teach unevenly and favour some students. Outside paid tutors or office hours, a student stuck on a textbook problem has nowhere to turn. Unanswered doubts pile up into the gaps that sink an exam.
challenge: Get a stuck student from a photo of the problem to understanding it, without handing them the answer.

title: The shop that cannot say what went missing
problem: In April 2025 a retailer with several stores found that stock discrepancies varied wildly from store to store on identical software, because staff counted carelessly. When the inventory module itself throws errors, support staff keep changing and every ticket starts from scratch. Small shop owners have stopped reporting shoplifting because police never respond, so the losses go unrecorded.
challenge: Make a full stock count take an hour and come out right, so a shop knows exactly what went missing.

title: Code is cheap; knowing what to build is not
problem: Since coding agents made building cheap in 2025, the hard part is deciding what to build, and that is still guesswork. Aspiring builders struggle to find problems people would pay to have solved, and keyword research says nothing about unmet needs. Inside companies, every client request arrives labelled top priority, so product managers get noise instead of evidence.
challenge: Turn a pile of customer requests and public complaints into a ranked list of what to build, with the evidence attached.

title: Destroying good clothes because nobody saw demand coming
problem: Garment makers produce on guesswork and lose heavily every year to unsold stock and clearance markdowns, and some brands destroy wearable excess rather than discount it, to protect their prices. Smaller makers cannot even see what is selling: in August 2026 an apparel manufacturer found Zoho Inventory's reports too rigid and its mobile version too limited for the factory floor.
challenge: Help a small apparel maker cut next season's unsold stock by a fifth.

title: Ghee that arrives already expired and growing fungus
problem: In a June 2026 survey, 48% of Indian online grocery shoppers could not see best-before dates before checkout, and near-expiry deliveries were common. Bread has arrived with no manufacturing or expiry date printed at all, and ghee from a quick-commerce dark store arrived already expired and growing fungus, in a home with a young child.
challenge: Catch every expired or undated pack before it reaches a customer's door.

title: Fixed-price orders meet metal prices that never sit still
problem: Small engineering, plastics and component makers quote fixed prices weeks before buying aluminium, copper, steel or polymer, then watch input costs jump. Margins on orders already won vanish, and metal buyers can wait months for material they cannot buy direct from mills.
challenge: Help a small manufacturer quote and buy so that a price spike cannot wipe out an order.

title: One coach, a separate payment link for every package
problem: Online coaches cannot show all their packages on one page, so each needs its own payment link, and clients have no booking view to see when a session is free. Coaching software keeps moving key features into paid add-ons, and when a session is missed, rescheduling is a tedious round of calls. These complaints came from 3 different coaches in 3 days of July 2026.
challenge: Let a solo coach sell any package, take payment and fill the calendar from one link they share.

title: Driver cancels, and the rider pays the fee
problem: Drivers demand more than the fare shown, in one case nearly 50% more, then cancel when the rider refuses, and the rider is charged the cancellation fee. Some take cash for the trip and then mark it cancelled, so the rider pays twice. Riders told the same story in June, September and October 2025.
challenge: Make sure the person who cancels a ride is the one who pays for it.

title: Hijacked channels and a support desk that cannot help
problem: When a creator account is hijacked, moved between owners or caught in a login loop, recovery options are already changed and support cannot restore access. A small media team can lose a channel it spent years building, along with the earnings attached to it.
challenge: Get a locked-out creator back in control within days, and make the next takeover far harder to pull off.

title: Flying blind on next month's cash
problem: Standard small-business accounting software has no basic cash forecast, so owners build spreadsheet workarounds to see what is coming. In July 2026 merchants found settlements landing later than expected, which made day-to-day cash planning harder still. Growing firms need senior financial planning help but cannot afford a full-time finance head.
challenge: Show a small owner, each morning, how much cash they will have in 30 days.

title: Nobody will come to fix one switchboard
problem: Homeowners cannot get electricians to come for small jobs like a fan or switchboard because they prefer big contracts, and a night-time plumbing emergency means paying inflated rates for whoever answers. People who would fix things themselves lack experienced local help, and a tiny repair turns into a store trip plus research into paints, fillers and tools. Small faults linger for weeks.
challenge: Get a household's small repair diagnosed by video and either fixed by them or by someone nearby today.

title: The best courses are only in English
problem: Bright students outside big cities miss top online courses because most are available only in English. Learners of less common languages can barely find beginner reading material, and flashcards drill the same sentences instead of fresh audio examples. Indian-language speech models matured in 2025, yet good teaching still rarely arrives in the language a learner thinks in.
challenge: Turn one strong English course into one a student who thinks in an Indian language learns from just as well.

title: Packaging costs and rules that shut out tiny sellers
problem: Micro sellers face thousands of euros a year in packaging registration fees before their first sale in the EU, and one tiny repair-and-resale shop has stopped shipping there altogether. At home, Indian beauty brands saw packaging component costs jump 60–70% within weeks in March 2026, before they could raise prices. Customers, meanwhile, open single small items in boxes far too big for them, stuffed with plastic.
challenge: Cut a small seller's packaging cost and paperwork per order by a third, at home and abroad.

title: Customers who never say what went wrong
problem: Local service businesses hear almost nothing back from customers, because long surveys go unanswered. Early-stage makers struggle to keep any regular feedback loop with the first people who try their work, and software firms have little feel for their non-technical customers' working day. Yet many Indian customers now prefer to talk in voice notes, not forms.
challenge: Get a local business honest feedback from a third of its customers, for under 30 seconds of their time.

title: The dress that looks nothing like its photo
problem: Clothes bought online often arrive in an off colour, thinner fabric or a worse fit than the photos showed, and price no longer signals quality, since cheap and expensive pieces both fall apart. On Meesho, products repeatedly differ from their listings, and one buyer of a poor-quality dress waited 20 days with no reply to their return request.
